prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Trailing her father, bearing his hand axe, the girl thought she had never guessed what earthly majesty was before then, as he strode unconcernedly holding a vicious gander by the horny mitts and let the big wings batter his knees. She was also surprised to feel a liberating satisfaction in the coming bloodshed, and that notwithstanding all the times she had been beleaguered and had fled, today she did not fear the barnyard hubub. Yet, as her father’s clever stroke fell, as the pronged head skipped sideways and the neck plumes stiffened with blood from the cleft, she was angry; and, when the headless goose ran to the brook and was carried off into the woods alive, she rejoiced, and subsequently frequented those woods and avoided her father. When the goose began to mend she brought him small hominy, which was welcome though she had to press the kernels one by one into the pink neck that throbbed into her palm; when haemorrhage occurred she would not spare handkerchiefs, and stanching the spot she felt a thrill of sympathy. But for the most part there was steady progress, and growing vigor was accompanied by restlessness, and one cool day the blind thing was batted out of existence by a motorcycle. She had no time for tears. She ran upstairs to miss her father’s barytone commiseration, then out onto the fields, and, holding an old red pinwheel, ran ran ran ran.

### Option 1: Literary & Atmospheric (Recommended)
*This version preserves the rich, gothic storytelling tone of the original while improving flow, rhythm, and diction.*

She was surprised to discover a liberating satisfaction in the impending bloodshed, realizing that despite all the times she had been cornered and forced to flee, she no longer feared the barnyard clamor. 
>

When the headless goose fled to the brook and was carried alive into the woods, she secretively rejoiced; thereafter, she haunted those trees and avoided her father.

Whenever hemorrhaging occurred, she spared no handkerchiefs, feeling a thrill of deep sympathy as she stanched the wound. For the most part, his recovery was steady, yet his growing vigor brought a restless energy—until one cool day, the blind creature was abruptly struck down by a motorcycle.

Following behind her father while carrying his small hatchet, the young girl felt she was witnessing a grand, regal power unlike anything she had known before. Her father stepped along indifferently, gripping a fierce male goose by its tough, webbed feet while the bird's massive wings beat repeatedly against his legs. Surprisingly, the prospect of the impending slaughter gave her a sense of unburdened satisfaction; despite her past experiences of being harassed and fleeing from farm animals, the loud chaos of the yard failed to intimidate her on this day.

However, when her father delivered a skillful strike—sending the bird's pointed head bouncing to the side as blood soaked into the stiffening neck feathers around the wound—she was filled with outrage. Her anger turned to joy when the neckless gander scrambled toward a stream and drifted into the surrounding forest, still very much alive. From that moment on, she routinely spent her time wandering those woods while keeping her distance from her father.

As the goose began to heal, she nourished it with small bits of corn. The bird received the food gladly, though she had to press each grain individually into the raw, pink throat opening that pulsed against her palm. Whenever bleeding recurred, she freely used her handkerchiefs to stem the flow, feeling a surge of deep compassion during those moments. 

Overall, the creature made steady progress, though its renewed strength was accompanied by growing restlessness. Ultimately, on a chilly afternoon, the sightless animal was struck and killed by a passing motorcycle.

Without pausing to cry, the girl dashed up to the house's upper floor to avoid her father's deep-voiced offers of sympathy. She then ran outside into the open countryside and, clutching an old red paper windmill, sprinted endlessly across the fields.

For as long as she could remember, the girl had viewed her father as a towering, infallible figure. So, on the crisp morning he finally decided to put an end to the farm’s troublesome gander—a territorial, aggressive bird that had terrorized the yard for months—she felt a surge of childish pride. Walking briskly beside him toward the chopping block, she carried a sense of excited satisfaction. To be included in this adult chore felt like a rite of passage, an invitation into her father’s brave, pragmatic world.

That excitement evaporated in a single, terrifying instant. 

When her father brought down the heavy blade, the strike was brutal but imprecise. Blood sprayed across the frosty grass, but instead of falling still, the horribly mangled bird thrashed wildly. Blindsided by the grotesque violence, the girl felt her admiration curdle into immediate, burning anger toward her father. Before he could strike again, the bird—blinded, bleeding, its head half-severed and hanging at a sickening angle—scrambled to its feet and made a desperate, chaotic dash into the dense pine woods bordering the property. As her father cursed and gave chase into the underbrush, the girl stood frozen, secretly rejoicing in the creature's improbable escape.

In the days that followed, a quiet cold war settled over the household. The girl pulled away from her father, refusing his smiles and shrinking from his touch. Her heart had migrated entirely to the forest. 

Deep in the woods, she found the gander tucked into the hollow of an old oak. Against all odds, the bird had survived the initial shock, though the blow had left it permanently blind and scarred. Every afternoon, the girl snuck away to her secret sanctuary. She brought soft rags to clean its crusted wounds and fed it steaming bowls of hominy, gently coaxing the bird to eat from her hands. Over weeks of patient care, a strange, quiet trust bloomed between the scarred creature and the sullen girl. 

Gradually, the goose began to thrive. Though sightless, it learned the contours of the forest clearing and the sound of her footsteps. It regained its vigor, lifting its neck to honk softly whenever she approached, its steady progress a daily victory against her father’s cruelty. 

Then came a clear Saturday afternoon. The girl was sitting near the edge of the woods where the trees met the quiet rural road, watching the gander stretch its wings and waddle confidently through the tall grass. It was stronger than it had ever been. But as the bird strayed a few feet closer to the gravel shoulder, the silence was shattered by the high-pitched roar of an engine. 

A motorcycle rounded the blind curve at full speed. There was no time to react, no time to scream. In a blur of chrome and dust, the bike struck the gander, killing it instantly before speeding off into the distance. 

The girl rushed to the roadside, kneeling beside the lifeless heap of white feathers. The miracle she had built with her own hands was undone in a fraction of a second, not by her father’s axe, but by pure, indifferent chance.

Hearing the commotion, her father hurried out from the house. When he saw what had happened, his face softened with pity, and he stepped forward, extending a hand to offer comfort. But the girl could not bear the warmth of his sympathy—to her, the blood on the road was just the delayed completion of what he had started weeks ago. 

Unable to look at him, she turned and bolted. She grabbed a bright, cheap pinwheel left leaning against the porch railing and ran blindly into the open pastures. With tears streaming down her face, she sprinted through the high wild grass, holding the toy aloft, watching its colorful blades spin frantically against the wind as she tried to outrun her grief.

The old grey gander had been the tyrant of the farmyard for as long as Clara could remember. It was a cruel, heavy-bodied bird with cold yellow eyes and a serrated bill that had left purple bruises on Clara’s ankles and torn the skirts of her aprons. But when her father finally took the bird by the neck and dragged it to the chopping block behind the woodshed, Clara felt no satisfaction—only a sudden, cold dread.

Her father was tired that afternoon. His hands were calloused and stiff from a long season of clearing timber, and his swing was rushed. The hatchet came down off-center, a sickening, dull thud that failed to cleave clean. 

Instead of ending the bird’s life, the blow struck high, severing the upper beak and eyes, leaving only a jagged, bleeding stump anchored to the lower brainstem. Shrieking a wet, horrible sound, the gander tore itself from the father’s grip. It flapped wildly, spraying crimson across the woodpile, and vanished into the thick underbrush at the edge of the property.

Her father cursed, wiped his blood-splattered brow with the back of a dirty sleeve, and spat into the dust. "Let it go," he muttered, tossing the hatchet into the grass. "It’ll bleed out in the pines by nightfall."

Clara stared at him. It wasn't just that he had failed; it was the casual, lazy indifference with which he turned his back on the suffering he had caused. A fissure opened in Clara’s heart, small but deep, dividing the man she had obeyed from the man he truly was.

She did not follow him inside for dinner. Instead, she slipped into the shadows of the woods, following the erratic trail of trampled ferns and dark, sticky droplets. 

She found the gander crouching beneath a hollow log. It was trembling violently, its neck a ruin of torn flesh and scabbing blood, yet its chest still heaved with ragged breath. The sight was horrific, a nightmare made of feathers and bone, but Clara felt a fierce, desperate impulse to undo what her father had done.

Using an old milk crate and a wool blanket stolen from the porch, she fashioned a hidden shelter in a dense thicket of wild blackberry brambles. Day after day, Clara returned to the woods in secret. She used an eyedropper to flush warm, salted water down the raw opening of its throat, followed by thin mashes of cornmeal and soaked grain. 

Remarkably, the bird survived. The wound knit into a smooth, hairless knot of pink scar tissue. Without eyes or a beak, the gander became entirely reliant on Clara. It learned the rhythm of her footsteps, stepping out from the brambles with uncertain, high-kicking strides, leaning its warm, feathered body against her knees as she sat on the pine needles. It was no longer a tyrant; it was a fragile, monstrous secret that belonged only to her.

As the weeks passed, the distance between Clara and her father widened into a canyon. At the kitchen table, she watched his heavy hands pass the bread, the same hands that had botched the kill, and she found she could no longer speak to him. When he asked her why she was so quiet, why she spent her afternoons wandering the edge of the timber, she only stared at her plate until he sighed and turned away, frustrated by her silence. Her refusal to forgive him became her quiet crusade.

By late autumn, the air turned bitter, and the ground froze into iron. The gander was strong enough to walk farther now, following Clara’s scent like a blind phantom through the trees. 

One afternoon, as Clara was returning to the hideout with a jar of warm mash, she heard the bird wandering out past the safety of the treeline. It had strayed onto the narrow gravel road that flanked their property, disoriented by the crisp, echoing wind.

Clara dropped the jar and ran. "No!" she cried out, her voice thin in the cold air.

From around the sharp bend of the hill came the sudden, deafening roar of an engine. A local boy on a heavy, retrofitted motorcycle rounded the curve, kicking up a cloud of loose stone. 

It happened in a fraction of a second. The rider swung wide, the iron exhaust pipe caught the blind bird square in the chest, and there was an explosion of grey down and shattered bone. The motorcycle wobbled, corrected itself, and sped off into the distance, leaving behind only the smell of gasoline and burnt rubber.

Clara reached the road and fell to her knees in the dirt. The gander was broken beyond repair, its body crushed into the freezing gravel, truly dead this time.

The noise brought her father out from the barn. He trotted down the gravel driveway, wiping his oil-stained hands on a rag. He stopped a few paces away, taking in the scene—the feathers scattered in the wind, the dead, headless bird, and his daughter kneeling in the dirt.

"Clara?" he said, his voice hesitant, reaching out a hand toward her shoulder. "Is that... was that the same damned bird?"

He stepped closer, his face a mix of confusion and pity, extending a hand to pull her up. But as his shadow fell over her, Clara looked from the bloody streak on the road up to his reaching hand. The cycle of violence had simply finished what he had started, rendering all her secret love and careful nursing entirely pointless. 

She flinched away from his touch as if his skin burned. She stood up, refusing to look him in the eye, and stepped back out of his reach.

"Clara, wait—" he called out.

She didn't answer. She turned and ran, ignoring his shouts, tearing past the woodshed and the house, diving blindly into the tall, dead stalks of the high rye fields. She ran until her lungs burned and her legs gave out, collapsing into the dry grass where no one could see her, wrapping her arms around her chest, and weeping alone in the quiet, empty field.

The forest was growing dark, the evening mist **trailing** through the ancient pine trees like ghost-linen across the mossy floor. **She** walked alone, the damp chill biting through her worn canvas jacket, each breath forming a brief bloom of silver in the quiet air. 

Her feet were heavy from hours of climbing, bruised by the uneven stones of the mountain path, **yet** her eyes remained fixed on the narrow ridge ahead. She refused to look back down at the warm, safe valley she had left behind at dawn. 

Her thoughts kept drifting back to the morning, to the doubts that had threatened to keep her anchored. Everyone had warned her that the pass was treacherous this late in the season, their cautious voices **trailing** off into ominous predictions of frost and sudden storms. They believed she would turn around before reaching the tree line. 

And **yet**, standing now at the edge of the timberline, watching the first pale starlight spill across the jagged peaks, a quiet triumph began to settle in her chest. The wind roared softly, **trailing** a spray of dry snow off the high cliffs above. **She** paused, pulling her collar tight against the draft, bruised but unbowed. The summit was still miles away, and the coldest hours of the night lay ahead; **yet**, as she took another steady step forward, she knew she would not break.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short piece of Southern Gothic microfiction about a young girl who witnesses her father fail to butcher a gander, then secretly nurses the surviving headless bird in the woods.
counterfactuals.output:
Daddy’s hatchet struck crooked, severing the head but missing whatever kept the rage inside. He spat a dark stream of tobacco into the red clay, cursed the white, thumping mess, and retreated to the porch with his jar of moonshine. 

The gander didn’t fall. It staggered blind out of the sunlit yard, dragging a crimson ribbon through the tall broomsedge. 

Maybelle found it hidden in the wet hollow beneath a dying sweetgum, where Spanish moss hung low as old hair. Its neck ended in a raw, puckered knot that whistled softly with every damp breath. The goose had always been a mean thing, but now, stripped of its hiss, it shivered in the pines like a abandoned child.

She brought it cornmeal mush thinned with well-water, dropping the paste down the pink hole of its exposed throat with an eyedropper. The bird leaned its warm, headless stump against her collarbone, its heavy body vibrating with an impossible heart. 

Every evening, while Daddy snored off his liquor behind the torn screen door, Maybelle sat in the dark woods and stroked the blood-stiffened feathers. She washed the stump with boiled water and whispered secrets to the open air above its neck. She knew what it was to keep living after the best part of you had been chopped away, and she swore to keep them both hidden from the hatchet.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a story about a girl who secretly cares for a headless goose in the woods, feeding it hominy directly into its neck. Include an unexpected modern death for the bird and end with the girl running through a field with a red pinwheel to escape her father's sympathy.
counterfactuals.output:
The goose lived in the deep notch of the hollow, where the wild blackberry canes arched over a bed of damp, rotting oak leaves. It was an impossible creature. A rogue hatchet blow from her uncle’s farm three weeks ago had taken its head clean off above the base, yet the brainstem had somehow held on, stubborn and blind, keeping the lungs pumping and the heart hammering inside its heavy downy chest.

Every afternoon at four, when the shadows of the pines stretched long and bruised across the forest floor, Clara crept into the woods with a warm, grease-stained Tupperware container. 

Inside were swollen, pearly grains of hominy. 

She would sit cross-legged on the moss, pulling the nervous, shivering bird gently into her lap. It didn't have eyes to see her, nor a beak to hiss, but it recognized the weight of her hands. It would quiet, its webbed feet relaxing against her knees. 

Clara took a grain of hominy between her thumb and forefinger. Carefully, reverently, she tilted the bird’s soft, grey-feathered neck. The severed top was a strange, puckered ring of pale muscle and pink tissue, pinkish-white and clean. With delicate precision, she slipped the slick, heavy corn directly into the gullet. Then, with long, rhythmic strokes of her palm, she smoothed her hand down the length of the goose’s throat, pushing the hominy down until she felt the bird’s reflex swallow take over.

*Gurgle-plump.* 

The goose would stretch its long neck upward, a blind gesture of satisfaction, and Clara would smile. It was their secret—a grotesque, quiet miracle that belonged only to her. She didn't want it fixed. She didn't want it saved. She just wanted to feed it, to keep the warm heart thumping beneath the white feathers.

On a Tuesday, the air was hot and smelled of coming rain. Clara sat in the clearing, the Tupperware half-empty, the goose resting its damp, headless neck against the crook of her elbow as she guided the fourth grain of hominy down its throat.

Then came the sound. 

It wasn't a fox, nor a coyote, nor the wind. It was a high-pitched, angry, electric whine—a metallic scream that sliced through the peaceful rustle of the leaves. 

Before Clara could even tilt her head toward the canopy, a stray commercial delivery drone, rogue from a lost signal three miles away, plunged through the pine branches at fifty miles an hour. It was a sleek, matte-black quadcopter, its carbon-fiber rotors whirring like furious razor blades.

It crashed into the hollow with violent, mechanical precision. 

There was a wet, sickening *thwack*, a spray of pine needles, and the crackle of a crushed lithium battery. 

Clara didn't scream. She sat frozen, blinded by a cloud of gray feathers and shattered plastic. When the dust settled, the drone lay smoking in the moss, its red status light blinking frantically: *SIGNAL LOST. SIGNAL LOST.* 

Beneath its crushed frame, the goose was still. The bird hadn't just been killed; it had been pulverized by the blind, stray geometry of modern air traffic. White down clung to the melted plastic casing of the drone’s camera. Hominy lay scattered in the dirt like teeth.

Clara’s heart slammed against her ribs. She reached out with trembling, dirt-stained fingers, touching a single warm, lifeless wing.

"Clara?"

A voice broke the silence from the edge of the woods. It was her father, stepping through the brush, holding an axe he’d been using to clear fallen branches by the driveway. He stopped, taking in the scene: the smoking drone, the spilled hominy, the pale, headless body of the dead bird.

His face softened into a look of agonizing, suffocating adult comprehension. 

"Oh, baby," he breathed, stepping forward, his voice dripping with gentle, unbearable pity. He dropped the axe and lowered himself into the dirt, reaching out to wrap his large, calloused arms around her shoulders. "Oh, Clara... you were keeping it alive? Honey, it was already broken. It was suffering. You don't have to look at it anymore. Come here..."

His sympathy felt like a heavy woolen blanket thrown over her head on a humid day. It threatened to smother the sacred, terrifying beauty of what she had kept secret. He was going to explain it to her. He was going to make it simple, sad, and logical. 

He reached to pull her against his chest.

Clara recoiled. She scrambled backward on her hands and knees, tearing herself out of his reach. 

"Clara, wait—"

She didn't wait. She lunged to the edge of the clearing, snatching up the bright red plastic pinwheel she had brought with her days ago to mark the trail to the hollow. 

She broke into a dead sprint.

She burst out of the tree line and hit the open pasture, her boots pounding through the tall, dry goldenrod. Her father was shouting behind her, his voice full of soft, terrible concern, but she ran faster, pushing the air from her lungs until her chest burned. 

She thrust the red pinwheel high above her head as she ran. 

The wind caught the cheap plastic vanes, sending them spinning into a blurred, violent wheel of crimson. It whirred furiously against the air, a bright, flashing shield of pure motion that blocked out the woods, blocked out the smoking plastic, and drowned out the sound of her father calling her name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: In a rich, literary style reminiscent of Flannery O'Connor, write a vignette exploring a child's complicated shift in loyalty away from her father during a farm slaughter, focusing on uncanny sympathy for a mutilated animal.
counterfactuals.output:
The November sky hung over the county like the flat, gray bottom of a galvanized tub, holding down the smell of woodsmoke and wet rust. Pearl stood by the scalding barrel, her knees stiff inside her heavy denim stock-feed overalls, watching her father move through the steam like a prophet who had arranged the weather himself. 

To Pearl, turned nine that autumn, Mr. Culpepper was a man composed entirely of iron and dry leather. He spoke in the short, flat cadences of an unread testament, and when he walked, the frozen mud beneath his boots yielded not out of soft mercy, but because it recognized a superior hardness. Until that morning, Pearl had believed that if the sun failed to rise, her father would simply haul it up over the ridge himself with a block-and-tackle and a pair of pliers.

The sow was named Old Bess, though Mr. Culpepper disapproved of naming meat. She was a monstrous, sway-backed Berkshire with a hide the color of lard that had sat too long in a dark pantry. She knew the barrel; she knew the sharp, sour tang of the scalding water, and she refused the gate with a heavy, ancient stupidity. 

"Get behind her with the slat, Pearl," her father commanded. His breath bloomed white and vanished in the cold. 

Pearl stepped forward, her allegiance as crisp and unquestioned as the frost on the pigsty rails. But the execution was botched. 

Mr. Culpepper raised the heavy iron singletree—he preferred it to the bullet, which he said was an indulgence for soft-headed townmen—and brought it down between the sow’s small, pale eyes. But the sow jerked, and the iron struck sideways, shearing off the creature’s left ear and crushing the side of her snout into a wet, purple ruin. 

The sound that came out of the pig was not the squeal of a farm animal; it was the high, tearing shriek of a steam whistle on a runaway locomotive. The sow did not fall. She collapsed forward onto her knees, thrashing in the icy muck, spraying a violent, steaming crimson across the white frost. 

Mr. Culpepper swore—a sharp, ugly word that dropped out of his mouth like a dry toad—and swung again, but his heel slipped on the slick clover. He looked, for the barest second, absurd: a middle-aged man in grease-stained trousers losing his footing in the blood of an uncooperative brute.

Pearl stopped. The wooden slat fell from her numb fingers.

The sow was still breathing, sucking air through a shattered, bubbling snout. It pushed itself up on three legs, its ruined head lifted toward the zinc sky. The left side of its face was a horror of exposed red muscle and splintered bone, but out of the remaining right eye—small, black, and bright as a blackberry—the animal looked directly at Pearl.

It was not a look of pleading. Pleading belonged to humans, to soft things that believed in fairness. It was an eye of terrible, unblinking majesty. In its terrible, mutilated state, the sow seemed suddenly vast, older than the barn, older than her father’s dry prayers. It wore its agony not as a defeat, but as a heavy, royal garment. It possessed a dark, monstrous grace that had nothing to do with Mr. Culpepper or his iron singletree.

"Grab the rope, Pearl! Dammit, grab the rope!" her father barked, his voice thin and shrill against the quiet of the woods. He was scrambling in the dirt, his face red and flustered, his dignity leaking out of him like sap from a wounded pine. He looked small. He looked like an intruder.

Pearl looked from her father’s red, sweating forehead down to the sow. 

A cold, strange heat bloomed behind her ribs. The invisible thread that tied her to the back of her father’s coat snapped with a quiet, absolute finality. She saw him now not as the architect of the farm, but as a clumsy, noisy thief trying to steal something he didn't have the manners to kill cleanly.

The sow took a heavy, shuddering step toward the girl. Blood poured from its jaw in a thick, dark ribbon, painting the front of Pearl’s boots. Pearl did not move back. She felt an uncanny, terrifying impulse to bow, to reach out her bare hand and touch the mangled, sacred flesh of the thing that refused to die for Mr. Culpepper’s breakfast.

"Pearl!" her father yelled again, his voice cracking on the hard air.

She slowly crossed her arms behind her back, her small mouth setting into a line as flat and unforgiving as the horizon. She watched him struggle with the heavy animal, her eyes wide and dry, harboring a quiet, treasonous devotion for the bleeding god thrashing in the mud.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark surrealist story about a headless goose that survives in the forest and the child who takes care of it.
counterfactuals.output:
The axe had taken the eyes, the orange spoon of a beak, and the small, oily brain that remembered the geometry of south. But it had forgotten to tell the goose that it was dead. 

So the body remained in the Black-Spindle Woods. It stood on thick, webbed paddles that were the color of damp carrots, beneath a canopy so dense the daylight arrived only as a cold, greasy film. Where its head should have been, there was only a stem—a raw, puckered tube of pale velvet and pink cartilage, ringed with dried crimson like a sealed wax stamp.

The goose did not wander blindly. It navigated by the sound of water dripping off black moss and the pull of the earth’s iron core. Its heart beat slow and heavy in its broad chest, a wet pendulum swinging in the dark.

The child found it behind a knee of rotting birch. 

The child was six, or perhaps seventy—her age was hard to tell because her cheeks were round and smeared with soot, but her eyes were grey as river slate and stayed open too long without blinking. She wore a coat stitched from the pelts of grey squirrels, their tiny tails dangling like frozen tassels around her hem.

She did not scream when the headless white thing stepped out of the ferns. She simply reached into her pocket, pulled out a handful of mashed mulberries, and held them out.

The goose tilted its neck. The stump sniffed the air—or rather, the exposed windpipe shivered, drawing in the smell of sugar and wet wool. 

"Open," the child whispered. 

She used a hollow crow feather as a funnel. Gently, delicately, she inserted the quill into the goose’s open gullet and pushed the bruised berries down into the dark of its body. The goose’s chest shuddered. A wet, subterranean gulp echoed from deep inside its ribs—*thump-thump, shhh-k-k*—and the feathers along its spine rippled with satisfaction.

From that afternoon, they belonged to each other in the quiet way that rot belongs to timber.

Every morning, the child cleared the goose’s neck. Leaves fell into the hole while it slept under the roots of the weeping ash, and if she did not pick them out with her bone tweezers, the bird’s breath sounded like a dry bellows stuffed with straw. She would sit cross-legged on the damp needle-litter, holding the goose between her knees. The goose would press the smooth, flat stump of its neck against her collarbone, warm and pulsing, while she worked.

It was not a quiet bird. Though it had no tongue, the syrinx—the voice-box buried deep down near its lungs—was still intact. It spoke in strange, truncated tones. When it was afraid of the fox-shadows, the neck whistled like wind through a keyhole. When it was full of rain-water and crushed snails, it made a sound like a wet finger rubbing the rim of a crystal glass.

The child taught the goose how to dance. 

Under the pale, blind eye of the winter moon, she would clap her soot-stained hands in three-quarter time. The goose would lift its heavy white wings—broad as sailcloth, smelling of river mud and old fat—and tip-toe in circles around the mushroom rings. It had no face to show its joy, but its skin flamed pink beneath its down, and the open tube of its throat puffed white clouds of steam into the frost.

Sometimes, the forest tried to fill the empty space. 

One evening in late November, a cluster of pale, milky mushrooms sprouted around the rim of the goose's neck, forming a ring of soft, trembling caps where the head had been. The bird walked heavier that night, its movements slow and drunk on spores. 

The child sat by the river and plucked the mushrooms off one by one, weeping softly because the bird hissed in pain as the roots tore away from its meat. 

"You are a bird," she told the wet red stump, pressing cold river mud to the wounds to stop the bleeding. "You are not a tree. You are mine."

The goose shivered and tucked its neck beneath its wing, though there was no head to hide.

Winter came, turning the forest into a cage of ice. The villagers down in the valley—who lived in warm, smoke-filled huts and killed things cleanly—never came into the Spindle Woods. They knew that things without heads lived there, held together only by grief and moss. 

Food grew scarce. The rivers froze into thick sheets of greenish glass. The child’s cheeks lost their roundness; her squirrel-skin coat grew loose, the little frozen tails rattling like dry teeth against her shins.

She could no longer find snails or late berries. The goose stood over her in the hollow of a fallen oak, its great white body draped over her lap like a heavy wool blanket, keeping her blood from turning to ice.

One night, when the wind howled through the high boughs like a dying horse, the child looked at the open neck of the goose. The throat was clear, clean, and warm, exhaling tiny gusts of heat that smelled of old pond water and safety.

She reached out with her small, dirty thumb and traced the edge of the scar. 

"I am cold," she told the syrinx.

The goose did not move. It sank down onto its breast, spreading its wings wide over the frozen mud, opening the broad fan of its feathers like a door.

The child crawled beneath the white down. She pressed her face directly into the softness of its chest, right beneath the place where the neck began. She listened to the valve of the heart opening and closing—a heavy, brass bucket plunging into a deep well.

Slowly, carefully, she reached up and slipped her own small, cold head into the soft, hollow opening of the bird's white neck. 

It was warm inside. It smelled of dark water, of seeds waiting for spring, of a sky that had no need for eyes. 

When the sun finally broke through the Spindle Woods in April, melting the ice into black ribbons of sludge, the creature stood up from the hollow tree. 

It was tall and white, with broad, heavy wings that smelled of river fat. Where its head should have been, there was a girl’s face, pale and soot-smeared, framed by a thick ruff of downy feathers. Her grey eyes blinked once, twice, adjusting to the daylight.

She opened her mouth, and out came the song of a goose—high, clear, and ringing through the iron trees, searching for a south that no longer existed.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a story based on the following elements: a hand axe, a father's baritone voice, feeding hominy to a neck stump, a motorcycle accident, and a running child holding an old red pinwheel.
counterfactuals.output:
The hominy was still steaming, soft and swollen until the yellow kernels burst open like soggy teeth in the tin bowl. 

Eli sat on the edge of the wrap-around porch, the bowl resting on his knees. Next to him, seated in a high-backed rocker, was what remained of his brother, Roy. Roy wore his usual flannel shirt, buttoned to the top, though above the collar there was only a pale, puckered mound of scar tissue—a silent, featureless crown. In the center of the stump was a small, pink aperture that opened and closed with a rhythmic, wet sigh.

Eli scooped up a mound of warm hominy with a horn spoon. "Open up, Roy," he murmured. 

His own voice surprised him—a deep, resonant baritone he had inherited from their father. It was a voice built for calling cattle across foggy pastures or singing low, rumbling hymns in the back pew of the Methodist church. Hearing it now, Eli felt the ghost of his father standing behind him, heavy-handed and silent.

Gently, with a patience born of two years' nightmare, Eli pressed the tip of the spoon against the trembling slit. The tissue yielded. The hominy slipped down into the dark, unseen gullet with a faint, wet swallow. Roy’s fingers, thick and calloused, twitched against the armrests of the rocker.

Down in the overgrown yard, the dry grass swished. 

Eli looked up. His five-year-old daughter, Lily, was darting through the high weeds. She was a streak of faded calico and bare knees, running in wide, dizzying circles around the rusted hulk of an old tractor. In her right hand, raised high toward the heat-bleached sky, she held an old red pinwheel. Its plastic blades were notched and sun-faded to the color of dried brick, but as she ran, the wind caught them, turning the toy into a blur of red motion. *Whir-whir-whir-whir.*

Lily laughed, a bright, fragile sound that hung in the humid air before dying out against the wall of the pines.

Eli turned back to the bowl, his chest aching with a cold, familiar weight. 

He remembered the night the world had split open. Highway 9, wet with autumn rain. The roar of Roy’s vintage BSA motorcycle tearing through the dark. Eli had been following in the pickup, his headlights sweeping over the slick asphalt just in time to see the bike catch the gravel on the shoulder. 

The frame had flipped, throwing Roy headlong into the low steel guardrail. 

Eli had run from the truck, grabbing the small hand axe he kept under the bench seat—a light, sharp tool with a hickory handle, meant for clearing fallen branches off the logging roads. He had sprinted into the dark, screaming his brother's name, the axe heavy in his fist, ready to chop through vines or pry away twisted metal. But when he reached the wreck, the axe was useless. The guardrail had acted like a guillotine. 

The paramedics had taken the head away in a black bag. But the body—defiant, terrifyingly stubborn—had refused to stop breathing. Its heart kept beating. Its lungs kept drawing air. When the hospital finally gave up and sent the silent, headless husk home, Eli had taken it in. It was his blood. It was all he had left of the boy who had built this cabin with him.

Leaning against the porch post right beside Roy’s rocker was that same hand axe. The steel blade was polished now, free of rust, reflecting the pale sun. Eli kept it close. Some nights, when the low, wet wheezing from the rocker kept him awake, he would hold the hickory handle and wonder if true mercy required one last strike. But he could never raise it. 

"One more, Roy," Eli whispered, his baritone rumbling soft and low, vibration humming in his throat like a purring motor. He filled the spoon again, leaning in close. "Just a bit more. Then we'll rest."

The body in the rocker shifted. The pale, scarred stump dilated, accepting the hominy. 

Out in the yard, Lily caught the wind just right. She sprinted toward the porch, the old red pinwheel spinning so fast it seemed to vanish entirely, leaving only a circle of crimson air. 

"Look, Daddy! Look how fast!" she cried, her little feet pounding up the porch steps. 

Eli forced a smile, his deep voice wrapping around her like a blanket. "I see it, baby. You're catching the storm."

She stopped beside the rocker, breathless, and held the red pinwheel over Roy’s lap. The breeze from its spinning blades ruffled the flannel of the headless man's shoulders. For a fraction of a second, the pink mouth in the stump tightened, as if listening to the whirring toy, remembering the feel of the wind on a open highway.

Eli set the empty bowl aside, rested his hand on the smooth knob of the axe handle, and listened to the steady, quiet rhythm of his home: the wind in the pines, the spin of the red wheel, and the soft, impossible breathing of the unburied dead.
